This post grew out of my diploma thesis in Quantum Information, which
I wrote in Hannover in 2010. The thesis was about quantum memory
channels, and in particular about how deep their memory runs.
Somewhere inside that work a smaller, self-contained question fell
out: how finely can you divide the most destructive process there
is?

The original is written for examiners, not for curious readers.
LLMs have made rewriting an old piece of mathematics a far smaller
job than it used to be, and I could not resist the temptation. So
here is the result again, redone with agentic support: the terse
notation of a thesis traded for pictures, worked examples, and a
slower pace, so that a motivated undergraduate can follow every
step.

The route, roughly: devices with memory give the problem its
physical face, the classical world gives a first answer, and the
quantum world a quadratically bigger one. Finally, we settle into a
small subclass of channels, simple enough to parameterize by hand,
yet powerful enough that in prime dimensions it comes within a
factor of two of the full quantum answer: the Clifford channels.

Worth flagging in advance: the room for slow erasure does not come
from the size of the space of quantum channels. It comes from a
small plane with finitely many points that secretly knows how to
multiply, and from a single matrix that drives every point of that
plane, except the centre, around one grand cycle. A mirror symmetry
cuts that cycle in half; that is the factor of two.

Enjoy the read.
